attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense observation. The phrase 'which LLMs essentially are' comes from the sentence just before it in the post. Nothing is hedged, and the drafter kept both parts of the claim.

contract.note: The plain reading (coherent state-and-rule models used reliably, including on unfamiliar cases) is an ordinary reading of 'proper world models', given the surrounding text. Marcus set no threshold and did not say whether purpose-trained sequence models count, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed, dated before the post. A next-token Othello model trained on synthetic games passes the coherence tests and stays robust under detours. This is narrow counterevidence. The same study finds incoherence in other models and domains.

July 2025 benchmark: frontier LLMs fall short of humans at prediction, planning and change detection in unfamiliar environments. Supports a practical limitation, but exploration and reasoning are confounds.

2024 chess next-token models reach a high legal-move rate and have probe-decodable board state. This counts against the idea that such models have no state model at all, but does not show broad, reliable use.
March 2025 preprint: fine-tuned LMs struggle to generate several consecutive legal Othello moves, even though they learn board representations.

reviews.rationale: The evidence points both ways. Frontier LLMs fail in unfamiliar environments (e2, e4), but a synthetic-Othello next-token model shows a coherent, robust world model (e1). Neither side meets its contract condition. The support condition needs representative coverage. The contradiction condition needs scope that matches the post's everyday world modeling, which narrow game domains do not show. The packet's own stated gaps admit this, so the packet does not settle the claim.
